results.name: common_factor_rule_gap
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples share a greatest common divisor g>=3, the yes rate for targets divisible by g minus the yes rate for targets not divisible by g; observed > model means people generalize a shared "multiples of g" rule more than pairwise exemplar divisibility/digit similarity predicts.

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response across all trials; a nonzero observed value vs a near-zero model value means the yes tendency drifts over the session (fatigue/learning), which the stationary model cannot produce.

results.name: same_decade_near_gap
results.description: Among targets 1-9 away from their nearest example, the yes rate when the target shares the tens digit (decade) with that nearest example minus when it does not; observed > model means people use a decade/tens-digit feature the model lacks (it codes only magnitude, final digit, parity, divisibility).
results.code:
# name: same_decade_near_gap
# description: Among targets 1-9 away from their nearest example, the yes rate when the target shares the tens digit (decade) with that nearest example minus when it does not; observed > model means people use a decade/tens-digit feature the model lacks (it codes only magnitude, final digit, parity, divisibility).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    d = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    d = np.where(np.isnan(d), np.inf, d)
    j = np.argmin(d, axis=1)
    near = ex[np.arange(len(t)), j]
    dmin = d[np.arange(len(t)), j]
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dec = lambda v: np.minimum(v // 10, 9)  # 100 grouped with 90s
    m = (dmin >= 1) & (dmin <= 9)
    same = dec(t) == dec(near)
    a, b = m & same, m & ~same
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: recency_last_vs_first
results.description: Among multi-example sets, the yes rate for targets numerically closer to the last-shown example than to the first, minus the yes rate for targets closer to the first; the model predicts a positive recency gap, so observed < model means people weight examples less by recency (or show primacy) than the model assumes.
results.code:
# name: recency_last_vs_first
# description: Among multi-example sets, the yes rate for targets numerically closer to the last-shown example than to the first, minus the yes rate for targets closer to the first; the model predicts a positive recency gap, so observed < model means people weight examples less by recency (or show primacy) than the model assumes.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    f, l = {}, {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        f[s], l[s] = ex[0], ex[-1]
    F = sets.map(f).to_numpy(); Lv = sets.map(l).to_numpy()
    k = (sets.str.count(",") + 1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dl, dfi = np.abs(t - Lv), np.abs(t - F)
    m = k >= 2
    a, b = m & (dl < dfi), m & (dfi < dl)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: prime_rule_gap
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all prime, the yes rate for odd prime targets minus odd non-prime targets; observed > model means people pick up a "prime numbers" category that the exemplar similarity features (magnitude, digit, parity, divisibility) cannot represent.
results.code:
# name: prime_rule_gap
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all prime, the yes rate for odd prime targets minus odd non-prime targets; observed > model means people pick up a "prime numbers" category that the exemplar similarity features (magnitude, digit, parity, divisibility) cannot represent.
def test_statistic(df):
    primes = set(p for p in range(2, 101) if all(p % q for q in range(2, int(p ** 0.5) + 1)))
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    allp = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        allp[s] = len(ex) >= 2 and all(x in primes for x in ex)
    m = sets.map(allp).to_numpy().astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isp = np.isin(t, list(primes))
    odd = t % 2 == 1
    a, b = m & odd & isp, m & odd & ~isp
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: hull_inside_minus_outside
results.description: Among sets with >=2 examples spanning a range of >=10, the yes rate for targets strictly inside [min,max] of the examples minus targets outside it; observed > model means people use an interval/range rule with a sharper inside-vs-outside boundary than graded magnitude similarity predicts.
results.code:
# name: hull_inside_minus_outside
# description: Among sets with >=2 examples spanning a range of >=10, the yes rate for targets strictly inside [min,max] of the examples minus targets outside it; observed > model means people use an interval/range rule with a sharper inside-vs-outside boundary than graded magnitude similarity predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    lo, hi = {}, {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        lo[s], hi[s] = min(ex), max(ex)
    L = sets.map(lo).to_numpy(); H = sets.map(hi).to_numpy()
    k = (sets.str.count(",") + 1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = (k >= 2) & (H - L >= 10)
    ins = m & (t > L) & (t < H)
    out = m & ((t < L) | (t > H))
    if ins.sum() == 0 or out.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[ins].mean() - r[out].mean())

results.name: within_set_gradient_sharpness
results.description: Mean, over sets with >=4 distinct targets, of the variance of per-target yes rates within the set; observed > model means people's generalization across targets of the same set is more all-or-none (rule-like, extreme) than the model's graded similarity predicts, observed < model means flatter.

results.name: set_size_yes_drop
results.description: Yes rate on single-example sets minus yes rate on sets of 3-4 examples; observed > model means people narrow their generalization with more examples (size-principle-like) more than the normalized exemplar familiarity predicts.
